content: 1. Healthcare staff and community health workers should be trained to screen for the need for psychological support and to provide appropriate psychological interventions. This includes understanding how to refer patients to suitable support services. 2. Regular monitoring and supervision of healthcare staff and community health workers providing psychological support are essential to ensure quality and consistency. 3. Psychosocial support groups should be established for individuals with lymphatic filariasis (LF) to share experiences and provide mutual support. These groups can be integrated across various disease conditions. 4. Social mobilization campaigns should be organized to raise awareness about the potential psychological impact of chronic complications of LF. 5. Efforts should be made to reduce the social stigma associated with LF through social mobilization campaigns. Discussions on social inclusion and income-generating activities should be held with welfare or financial services. 6. The socioeconomic needs of individuals with LF should be assessed, and preliminary social support should be provided by integrating them into existing income-generating activities through welfare services. 7. District health facilities should act as technical referral centers, providing access to treatment for complicated cases, offering expertise to communities, and conducting training and supervision for community health workers. They should also monitor and evaluate activities. 8. In areas with a high disease burden, specific LF teams of health staff should be formed. LF committees can also be established at the implementation unit or peripheral level to strengthen the capacity of government staff to engage communities and implement activities. 9. Community-based care strategies should be prioritized in areas where home-based care is chosen as the service delivery model. Community teams with diverse professional profiles should be established to improve the status of LF patients in their communities. 10. Stakeholders involved in implementing and supervising morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP) activities at the community level should align with those at the national level. If necessary, a situation analysis similar to that at the national level can be conducted at the implementation unit. 11. At the start of the program, the number of lymphoedema patients and those with suspected hydrocele should be estimated using various patient estimation approaches, such as pre-MDA census data. 12. Men with hydrocele should be referred to health workers for accurate diagnosis and offered surgery if needed. The geographical distribution of patients should also be determined. 13. Information on potential community health workers should be collected to form a managerial team, delivery strategy, and referral system for lymphoedema management. 14. The possibility of integrating long-term lymphoedema management activities with other home-based care programs should be explored. 15. Training for healthcare staff and community health workers should be organized at national or subnational levels. A cascade training model can be implemented, where district health workers train community health workers, who in turn train patients and their families. 16. For hydrocele management, national-level trainers should train regional and district-level physicians and surgeons. Medical officers must be trained in diagnosis, surgical fitness evaluation, and all aspects of surgery, including local anesthesia, postoperative care, and follow-up. 17. A follow-up system should be established to ensure regular visits to lymphoedema patients or their attendance at health facilities for routine care. Regular supervision should be organized until health workers can accurately record data in the patient tracking system. 18. Medications for treating acute attacks, such as antibiotics, antiseptics, antibacterial and antifungal creams, analgesics, and anti-inflammatory drugs, should be supplied to the most peripheral health facilities. 19. Reports from community health workers and health centers should be collected and summarized. Annual refresher training should be organized at least every two years to ensure the sustainability of lymphoedema management activities. 20. Hydrocelectomy services should be made accessible to patients as close to their location as possible. If surgical services are unavailable at the district level, they should be provided at the next highest level with consistent surgical services. 21. The estimated number of hydrocele cases should be determined, and community leaders and health workers should inform individuals about the availability of hydrocelectomy. Training for hospital medical staff responsible for hydrocelectomy should be organized, and monitoring and reporting should be conducted according to national program guidelines. 22. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of MMDP programs are critical. The M&E framework should guide countries in collecting data for elimination dossiers, monitoring progress, and evaluating the impact of national MMDP programs over time. 23. Specific indicators should be reported to WHO for submission of the country dossier for LF elimination and annual reporting to the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF). Countries should also develop additional indicators to objectively measure the success of MMDP components based on program design. 24. National programs should ensure that reporting tools and systems are developed to collect indicators required for WHO reporting. Additional indicators and tools specific to program designs and objectives should also be developed. 25. Data collection and reporting should be managed by the national program manager, with implementation units responsible for aggregating and transmitting data from health centers. Monitoring indicators for LF MMDP should include program coverage, training, and lymphoedema and hydrocele activities. 26. To monitor progress toward elimination, countries can use indicators such as the proportion of implementation units with completed patient estimations, the proportion of units providing MMDP care, and the proportion of units conducting quality-of-care surveys for lymphoedema and hydrocele management. 27. National programs should collect morbidity management and disability prevention data regularly, at least annually, and provide this data to WHO through the Epidemiological Data Reporting Form (EPIRF). 28. Reporting by public health centers through reporting units to the focal point for MMDP in national LF elimination programs should be streamlined. Monitoring involves routine data collection on all aspects of the program, with indicators collected at individual, community, or health facility levels depending on program design. 29. National programs are encouraged to sample at least 10% of facilities nationwide providing lymphoedema management or hydrocelectomy services to assess the quality of health services for these conditions. 30. Annual reporting to GPELF should include data on morbidity management and disability prevention, with information submitted to WHO through regional program review groups.
